notes.title: 대청소
notes.text: Korean homes do a big cleaning (대청소) before holidays and at the change of seasons. Floors get special care because people sit, eat and sometimes sleep on them.

lessons.goal: Say something happened completely (and maybe badly) with -아/어 버리다.

notes.title: 깨다 vs 깨지다
notes.text: Many Korean verbs come in pairs: one where someone does it (깨다 to break something, 열다 to open something) and one where it just happens (깨지다 to get broken, 열리다 to come open). Korean speakers often use the second kind to sound less blaming: 접시가 깨졌어요 ("the plate broke").

notes.title: -아/어 있다 vs -고 있다
notes.text: -고 있다 is an action in progress (문을 열고 있어요: "I'm opening the door"). -아/어 있다 is the state that remains afterward (문이 열려 있어요: "the door is open").

notes.title: 분리수거
notes.text: Korea has strict recycling rules (분리수거): paper, plastic, cans, glass and plastic film are separated, and food waste goes in special bags or bins. Regular trash goes in official pay-per-bag bags (종량제 봉투).

notes.title: 온돌
notes.text: Korean homes are heated through the floor (온돌, ondol), traditionally by fire and today by a boiler (보일러). That's why people sit and sleep on the warm floor in winter — and why 보일러 틀어 ("turn on the heat") is such a common phrase.
